items.title: Act and rule utilitarianism give different answers
items.claim: What is the distinction between act and rule utilitarianism?

options.text: They are alternative names for the same theory

Act utilitarianism judges each action by its consequences directly; rule utilitarianism asks which rules, if generally followed, would produce the greatest happiness — and applies those rules even when an individual act might seem to maximise utility differently
Act utilitarianism is the only legitimate form

items.reveal:
Jeremy Bentham's 'Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation' (1789) introduced the hedonic calculus. John Stuart Mill's 'Utilitarianism' (1861) distinguished higher and lower pleasures.

Rule utilitarianism (developed by R.M. Hare and Richard Brandt in the 20th century) attempts to address objections to act utilitarianism — that it permits horrific acts (killing one innocent to save five) and creates impossible decision burdens.

Critics argue rule utilitarianism collapses into act utilitarianism (just add 'except in special cases') or into Kantian deontology (just follow the rules).
items.why: Utilitarianism is not one theory. The act/rule distinction changes the answers radically — and exam answers that treat 'utilitarianism' as monolithic miss the most important internal debate.

items.title: Jihad has greater and lesser meanings in classical Islam
items.claim: What is the greater/lesser jihad distinction?

options.text: Both refer only to armed warfare

A widely cited hadith distinguishes lesser jihad (armed struggle in defence of the community) from greater jihad (inner struggle against one's own ego); the hadith's authenticity is debated but the inner-struggle understanding is found in independent Sufi and mainstream piety traditions
Jihad refers only to economic struggle

items.reveal:
The Arabic root j-h-d means 'to strive, to exert effort'. The greater/lesser distinction is attributed to a hadith reported by al-Bayhaqi and al-Khatib al-Baghdadi: 'We have returned from the lesser jihad to the greater jihad — the jihad against the self.'

Ibn Taymiyya (d. 1328) and some modern scholars question the hadith's chain of authentication. But the inner-struggle theme appears widely in Sufi writing and is not dependent on the hadith alone.

Classical Islamic law (fiqh) regulates armed jihad with conditions on declaration, conduct, and protection of non-combatants — distinct from later extremist appropriations of the term.
items.why: A word picked up by 21st-century media can carry meanings that don't match its theological tradition. 'Jihad' in classical Islam is far more various than its English-language press usage.

items.title: Modern Judaism has three or four main branches
items.claim: What are the main Jewish denominations?

options.text: One unified Judaism with no internal divisions

Orthodox (including Modern Orthodox and Haredi); Conservative (called Masorti in UK); Reform; Reconstructionist — distinguished mainly by their stance on the binding nature of Halakhah (Jewish law) and the role of modernity
Only ethnic, not religious, divisions exist

items.reveal:
Reform Judaism emerged in early 19th-century Germany (Israel Jacobson, Abraham Geiger), arguing for adapting tradition to modern reason. Orthodox responses (Samson Raphael Hirsch) defended strict observance of Halakhah while engaging with modern life.

Conservative/Masorti Judaism (Zacharias Frankel, Solomon Schechter at JTS New York from 1902) is a middle path — Halakhah binding but historically developing. Reconstructionist Judaism (Mordecai Kaplan, 1922) sees Judaism as evolving religious civilisation.

In Israel, the Chief Rabbinate is Orthodox and controls marriage and conversion law; in the US, Reform is the largest denomination by membership.
items.why: Religions are internally diverse. Judaism's denominational landscape sets up the central modern question — how do tradition and modernity relate? — in different ways.
